passage: Kalyani had been teaching at the private school in Sangli for three years on the same salary. When the principal, Harish-sir, offered her the job of exam coordinator, she almost said yes on the spot. Instead she went home and called two friends in similar roles in nearby towns to learn what coordinators usually earned. She wrote down the extra hours the job would take. The next morning she said, "I'd be glad to take it on. Given the extra work, I was hoping for a raise closer to this figure." She named a number a little higher than she expected to get. Harish-sir frowned, then offered something in between. She thanked him and asked for it in writing.

qa.q: How long had Kalyani been teaching at the Sangli school?
qa.a: She had been teaching there for three years.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani nearly say yes on the spot?
qa.a: She was probably pleased and flattered by the offer and didn't want to seem ungrateful.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do to prepare for the negotiation?
qa.a: She called friends in similar roles to learn usual pay and wrote down the extra hours the job would take.

qa.q: How might Harish-sir see Kalyani after this?
qa.a: He may see her as professional and prepared, since she asked politely and backed up her request.

grounding: Shows a young teacher preparing, naming a figure first and negotiating a raise respectfully.

passage: Vera got the offer from the design studio in Lisbon on a Tuesday. The salary was lower than she'd hoped, and she felt the familiar urge to just be grateful. Her friend Beatriz, who'd changed jobs twice, said, "Ask. The worst answer is no." Vera drafted an email three times. The final version thanked them warmly, said how excited she was, and mentioned the average salary for similar roles she'd found in a public survey. She asked if they could meet that, or add extra days of leave. Two days of silence made her stomach churn. Then the reply: they couldn't raise the salary much, but could add five days of leave and review her pay in six months. She accepted, smiling.

qa.q: What did the studio agree to add?
qa.a: They agreed to add five days of leave and review her pay in six months.

qa.q: How did Vera feel during the two days of silence?
qa.a: She felt anxious; her stomach churned while she waited.

qa.q: What made Vera's email effective without harming the relationship?
qa.a: She was warm and enthusiastic, used evidence and offered more than one option.

qa.q: What would have changed if Vera had just accepted the first offer?
qa.a: She would have missed the extra leave and pay review, and started the job feeling she'd undersold herself.

grounding: Shows a young designer negotiating terms politely with evidence and flexible options.

passage: Uday was two months into his job at a logistics company in Kolkata when HR offered him a permanent contract. Zeenat, a colleague who had joined a year earlier, noticed him reading it at his desk with a frown. "Something wrong?" she asked. The contract had a non-compete clause and no mention of the work-from-home days his manager had promised. "Ask before you sign," she said. "Nicely, but ask." Uday went to HR and said he was happy to sign, but wanted the home days written in and to understand the non-compete. The HR manager looked irritated at first, then checked with his manager. The home days were added. Uday thanked Zeenat with a box of sweets, relieved he hadn't stayed quiet.

qa.q: What was missing from Uday's contract?
qa.a: The work-from-home days his manager had promised were missing.

qa.q: What does Uday's frown while reading suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt uneasy about parts of the contract that didn't match what he'd been told.

qa.q: Which choice helped Uday most, and why?
qa.a: Raising the missing terms politely before signing, because once signed it would have been much harder to change.

qa.q: How might the HR manager's view have changed during the conversation?
qa.a: At first he seemed irritated, but after checking with Uday's manager he saw the request was fair and fixed it.

grounding: Shows a young worker reviewing contract terms and negotiating politely before signing.

Dear Irfan,
Thank you for the offer for the Data Analyst role. I'm genuinely excited about the team and the product, and I'd like to make this work.
Having looked at the role's scope, which includes managing the reporting pipeline and client dashboards, and at salary surveys for similar positions in Mumbai, I was hoping for a base salary closer to 11 lakh rather than the 9 lakh offered. I also bring two years of experience with the exact tools your team uses.
If the base is fixed, I'd be glad to discuss a review at six months, or support for a certification course.
I'm happy to talk this through on a call whenever suits you. Either way, I appreciate your time and our conversations so far.
Warm regards,
Abhinav

qa.a: Closer to 11 lakh, rather than the 9 lakh offered.

qa.q: Why does Abhinav open by saying the team and product are genuinely exciting?
qa.a: Abhinav wants Irfan to know the job is really wanted, so the request does not sound like a threat and the relationship stays warm.

qa.q: What makes Abhinav's email a good negotiation?
qa.a: Abhinav anchors with a researched figure, gives reasons tied to the role and to two years with the team's tools, offers alternatives if the base is fixed, and stays polite.

qa.q: How might Irfan read this email?
qa.a: As a reasonable, respectful request Irfan can take to the managers, rather than a demand that sours the hire.

grounding: An email shows a young professional preparing, anchoring and negotiating salary while protecting the relationship.

passage: Hafsa, you asked how I handled that first freelance contract. Badly, then better. The client asked, 'What's your rate, Nitin?' and I panicked and said a number way lower than I'd planned, just to seem easy to work with. The moment it left my mouth, I knew. That first number became the ceiling for everything after, which, I learned later, is called anchoring. So on the next project I prepared. I wrote down what similar designers charged, what the work involved, and my walk-away point. When the new client asked, I named my number first, a bit above what I needed, and explained what was included. They pushed back, and we met a little below it, still above my minimum. I also asked for the payment schedule and revision limits in writing. We still work together. Being clear didn't hurt the relationship at all. It made it calmer.

qa.q: What did Nitin do when the first client asked for a rate?
qa.a: Nitin panicked and named a number much lower than planned, to seem easy to work with.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel the moment that first number was said?
qa.a: Nitin regretted it immediately, knowing it was too low.

qa.q: What did Nitin prepare before the next negotiation?
qa.a: What similar designers charged, what the work involved and a walk-away point; then Nitin named a number first and got the terms in writing.

qa.q: How might the second client see Nitin's clear terms?
qa.a: As professional and trustworthy, which is why the working relationship stayed calm and ongoing.

grounding: A young freelancer describes learning to prepare, anchor first and negotiate terms without harming the relationship.

passage: I'm Siddharth, and I sat beside Alka in the hiring manager's cabin as her future teammate, so I saw her negotiate, though I can't tell you what she felt. The manager offered eleven lakh, the figure HR had set. Alka thanked him, genuinely. Then she opened a slim folder: three salary surveys for the role in Bengaluru, and her own list of two product launches, one of which she had led. "Based on this, I was expecting between fourteen and fifteen," she said, and stopped talking. The silence was long. I looked at my shoes. The manager said the budget was tight. Alka nodded. "I understand. If the base is fixed, could we look at a joining bonus or a review at six months?" They settled at thirteen with a six-month review. She shook his hand warmly. In the lift she let out one long breath, the only sign I saw.

qa.q: What salary did the manager first offer?
qa.a: Eleven lakh.

qa.q: What might Alka have been feeling during the long silence?
qa.a: Alka was probably tense but determined, holding the silence after naming her range; the long breath in the lift hints at relief.

qa.q: Which negotiation moves helped Alka while keeping the relationship good?
qa.a: She thanked him genuinely, anchored with evidence, stayed silent, and offered alternatives like a review when the base was fixed.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the negotiation from the outside?
qa.a: Siddharth was uncomfortable during the silence, staring at the floor, but seems impressed by how calm and warm Alka stayed.

grounding: A future teammate watches a young woman prepare, anchor and negotiate her salary without harming the relationship.

passage:
Two years ago. Afreen accepted her first job offer on the phone within a minute, grateful just to be asked. Three months later she learned that the man hired with her, same degree, earned twenty percent more. He had simply asked.
This January. A new offer came from a logistics firm in Gurgaon. The recruiter, Gurpreet, named a number and waited. Afreen said, "Thank you. Can I take two days to review?" Her heart was hammering, but Gurpreet said, "Of course."
Two days later. Afreen had checked salary data for the role, listed her results at her current job, and rehearsed with her sister. On the call she said, "I'm excited about the role. Given the market and my experience running the Jaipur warehouse, I was looking for eighteen." Gurpreet came back with sixteen and a half plus a relocation allowance. Afreen accepted, then sent a warm thank-you. Maybe she had left something on the table. Not twenty percent.

qa.q: How much more did the man hired with Afreen earn?
qa.a: Twenty percent more.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she asked for two days?
qa.a: Afreen felt nervous, heart hammering, afraid that asking might cost the offer.

qa.q: What preparation made Afreen's counter-offer credible?
qa.a: Checking salary data, listing concrete results like running the Jaipur warehouse, and rehearsing with her sister.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see Afreen after the negotiation?
qa.a: Gurpreet likely sees a prepared, professional candidate, especially after the warm thank-you, so the relationship starts well.

grounding: Across two job offers, a young woman moves from accepting instantly to preparing and anchoring a respectful salary negotiation.

passage: Gurleen, before you walk into that salary talk, let your Rukmini Aunty tell you how I nearly lost my best job. I was twenty-six, a pharmacist moving to a hospital chain in Pune. Someone had told me, "Always ask for more." So when they made the offer, I said, "Double it or I'm not coming." No reasons, no numbers. The HR head, a calm woman called Mrs Deshpande, went silent, then said, "Then perhaps we're not the right place." My stomach fell through the floor. I cried that night and called her back the next day. I apologised, and this time I came with reasons: my years at the old hospital, my night-shift experience, what others in the role earned. I asked for something specific and asked what flexibility she had. We met in the middle. We worked together fifteen years. So ask, Gurleen. But ask with reasons, and leave the door open.

qa.q: What did young Rukmini first demand?
qa.a: Double it or I'm not coming.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when Mrs Deshpande said they might not be the right place?
qa.a: Rukmini felt shocked and afraid, stomach falling, realising the ultimatum might cost the job.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it repair things?
qa.a: Calling back to apologise and returning with reasons and a specific ask, which showed respect and gave Mrs Deshpande something to work with.

qa.q: How might Mrs Deshpande have felt during the two calls?
qa.a: She was probably put off by the ultimatum, then pleasantly surprised by the apology and reasons, enough to meet in the middle.

grounding: An aunt tells a young woman how an ultimatum nearly cost her a job and how prepared, respectful negotiation repaired it.

The offer came at 3 p.m. with a line in bold: please confirm by 6 p.m. today. Mohit was at his cousin's engagement in a banquet hall with a band warming up.

He found a storeroom behind the kitchen, stacked with chairs, and called Mahima from HR. The line kept crackling.

"Thank you for the offer. I'm excited about the role," he said, pressing a finger to his other ear. "Before I confirm, I'd like to discuss the base pay. From what I've seen for similar roles in this city, a figure about ten percent higher would be fair for my experience."

Mahima paused. "The band is fixed for this level."

"I understand. Would a joining bonus or an earlier review, say at six months, be possible instead?"

"Let me check with my manager. I'll call back by five thirty."

At five twenty-five she did: a six-month review, in writing. Mohit thanked her twice, stepped back into the noise, and finally let out a long breath.

qa.q: By what time did the offer need to be confirmed?
qa.a: The offer needed to be confirmed by 6 p.m. today.

qa.q: How was Mohit feeling while he waited for Mahima's call back?
qa.a: He was probably tense and anxious about the deadline, which is why he let out a long breath of relief when she agreed.

qa.q: What worked about how Mohit negotiated under time pressure?
qa.a: He thanked Mahima, gave a researched reason for his ask, and when base pay was fixed, suggested other options such as an earlier review, keeping the tone friendly.

qa.q: How might Mahima see Mohit after the call?
qa.a: Mahima likely sees him as polite and prepared, someone who pushed for himself without making the call unpleasant, which is a good start to working together.

grounding: Under time pressure in a noisy place, a young candidate anchors a salary ask with research and negotiates alternatives while keeping the relationship warm.

The café near the metro was loud, but Jyoti had chosen it because it felt less like an office. Arohi, who would be her new manager, arrived with two coffees.

Jyoti had spent three evenings preparing. She had one page of notes: her current work, what the new role asked for, and the two things she wanted most.

"I'm really keen to join," she began. "I'd like to talk about two things: the title, and remote days."

Arohi nodded.

"The job description includes managing the two junior analysts. So I'd like the title to be senior analyst, not analyst. And I'd like two remote days a week; my commute would be almost two hours each way."

Arohi frowned slightly. "Two days is more than the team gets."

"Would one day to start, and a review after three months, work?"

Arohi smiled. "That, I can do. And I'll push for the title."

Jyoti's shoulders came down from somewhere near her ears.

qa.q: How many evenings did Jyoti spend preparing?
qa.a: Jyoti had spent three evenings preparing.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel by the end of the conversation?
qa.a: Jyoti felt relieved, as her shoulders finally relaxed after the tension of asking.

qa.q: What could someone learn from how Jyoti prepared for this negotiation?
qa.a: Link each ask to a real reason, like the managing duties or the long commute, and have a fallback ready, such as a trial with a review.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Jyoti's requests?
qa.a: Arohi seems to see them as reasonable and well argued, which is why she offers the trial day and agrees to push for the title.

grounding: A young professional negotiates role title and working terms with a future manager, anchoring with clear reasons and offering a compromise.

passage:
Kalyani put the draft contract on the table. "Before I sign, can we go through three things?"

Jyoti, the startup's founder, raised an eyebrow. "Sure."

"First, the scope. It says 'all design needs'. That could mean anything. Can we list it: the app screens, the logo, and two rounds of changes?"

"Fair. What else?"

"Payment. Right now it's all at the end. I'd like half at the start and half on delivery."

Jyoti frowned. "We're tight on cash this quarter."

"I understand. What about a third at the start, a third at the halfway review, and a third at the end?"

Jyoti tapped her pen. "Okay. That's doable."

"And last, if you want extra changes beyond two rounds, I charge per round. It's written at the bottom."

Jyoti laughed. "You came ready."

"I've been burnt before," Kalyani said. "I'd rather we both know where we stand, so we can still like each other at the end."

They shook hands.

qa.q: What did Kalyani ask to list in the scope?
qa.a: She asked to list the app screens, the logo, and two rounds of changes.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani say she "came ready" with these terms?
qa.a: Kalyani had been burnt before, so she was wary of vague contracts and wanted to feel secure while keeping a good relationship.

qa.q: What worked when Jyoti said cash was tight?
qa.a: Kalyani stayed calm and offered a middle option, splitting payment into three parts, which met both their needs.

qa.q: How does Jyoti experience the negotiation?
qa.a: Jyoti is a bit surprised and amused, but seems to respect Kalyani's clarity and ends on friendly terms with a handshake.

grounding: A young freelancer negotiates contract scope and payment terms with a client, finding compromises that protect both sides and the relationship.

passage:
When I got my first offer after my master's, I almost said yes on the phone. The HR person said a number, and I felt so grateful to be picked that I wanted to accept before they changed their minds.
My friend Ojas, who'd negotiated his own offer, stopped me. "Ask for a day. Then do your homework."
So I did. I looked up salary surveys for the role and city, and asked two seniors what they'd been offered. The number was at the bottom of the range.
I rehearsed with Ojas. The next day I said, "I'm really excited about this role. Based on the market range and my project experience, I was hoping for something closer to the middle of the range." My voice shook a bit.
They came back with a higher offer and an extra review after six months. I'm Yash, and I learned that asking politely isn't greedy.

qa.q: What did Ojas tell Yash to ask for first?
qa.a: A day, to do some homework.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when the first number was offered?
qa.a: Yash felt grateful and eager, so relieved at being picked that saying yes immediately was tempting.

qa.q: Which parts of Yash's preparation made the negotiation work without damaging the relationship?
qa.a: Researching the market, rehearsing, starting with enthusiasm and giving reasons for the request kept it polite and grounded.

qa.q: How might the HR person have seen Yash's request?
qa.a: The HR person probably saw it as normal and professional, since it was polite and based on market data.

grounding: Shows a young professional preparing and negotiating a salary offer respectfully.

Hiring manager's note. Darshan, operations lead.
We offered Jomon, 25, a team coordinator role. He thanked us and asked for two days. When he came back, he was prepared.
He didn't just ask for more money. He said he was excited about the role, then explained that his current job included managing vendors, which our role also needs, and that similar roles in the city paid more. He named a figure a little above what we'd planned, clearly as a starting point.
When I said the budget was fixed, he asked about other terms: a review after six months, two work-from-home days, and a training allowance. He stayed friendly the whole time.
We couldn't meet his figure, but we agreed on part of the gap, the six-month review and the training. I came away respecting him more, not less. I think he'll negotiate well with our vendors too.

qa.q: How many days did Jomon ask for before responding?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: How do you think Jomon felt going into the negotiation?
qa.a: Jomon likely felt nervous but confident, having prepared his reasons and alternatives.

qa.q: What negotiation skills did Jomon show?
qa.a: Jomon anchored with a researched figure, linked it to his experience, stayed friendly, and moved to other terms when salary was fixed.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Jomon after the negotiation?
qa.a: Darshan respects him more, seeing skills that will help with vendors too.

Wednesday
Ojas here. The contract from the start-up came today: good role, lower salary than I hoped, and a clause saying I can't work for any competitor for two years after leaving. Two years!
I was about to sign because I like the founders. Then I remembered what I told Yash last year: don't be grateful, be prepared.
So I called Nikita, the recruiter. I said I was excited, and asked two things. Could the salary be closer to what I'd earn elsewhere, since I'd lead the analytics? And could the non-compete be shorter or narrower?
Nikita said she'd check. I felt shaky after hanging up. I also emailed a lawyer friend of Papa's to read the clause, since I don't understand contract law.
Nikita called back: salary a bit higher, non-compete six months. I'm signing tomorrow.

qa.q: How long was the original non-compete clause?
qa.a: Two years.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel after hanging up with Nikita?
qa.a: Ojas felt shaky, nervous about having asked for changes.

qa.q: What did Ojas do right, and why was asking a lawyer important?
qa.a: Ojas prepared, stayed positive and asked for specific changes; asking a lawyer mattered because contract clauses need expert reading.

qa.q: How might the founders see Ojas's requests?
qa.a: They may see them as reasonable and professional, showing someone who reads carefully and knows Ojas's own worth.
